title: The pale blue dot
hook: a 1990 photograph from Voyager 1 shows Earth as a speck in a sunbeam

segments.voice: Yesterday Marcus rose above the city in his mind, what Hadot called the view from above. Your line was so small, so loved.

Marcus had to imagine the view from above. In 1990, people got to see it. A small spacecraft called Voyager 1 had been flying away from Earth since 1977. It had passed Jupiter and Saturn, and was heading out of the solar system forever. Its cameras were about to be switched off to save power. Before they were, the astronomer Carl Sagan and his colleagues persuaded NASA to do something with little scientific purpose: turn the camera around, and take one last picture of home.
screen: `VOYAGER 1, SINCE 1977.` → `LEAVING THE SOLAR SYSTEM.` → `TURN AROUND. ONE LAST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: On February 14, 1990, from about six billion kilometers away, nearly four billion miles, Voyager 1 took a series of pictures of the planets. In one, a band of scattered sunlight crosses the frame, and sitting in it is a single tiny dot, less than one pixel wide. That dot is Earth. Every ocean, every city, every person alive in 1990, inside a speck you could miss if a hair landed on the photo. Sagan wrote about it a few years later, in his book Pale Blue Dot. His words are too recent to quote here, so here's the gist, in plain words. Everything people have ever done, the wars and the lullabies, the empires and the kitchen tables, took place on that one pale speck, sitting in a stripe of sunlight. He drew two lessons from it. First, humility: the quarrels over who rules which corner of the dot look small from that far out. Second, responsibility: the dot is where we live, so the care of it, and of each other, falls to us, and to nobody else. It's Marcus's view from above, made real, with the same two halves. So small. So loved. Everyone, all of us, on one speck.
screen: `FEBRUARY 14, 1990.` · `LESS THAN ONE PIXEL.` · `EVERYONE WHO EVER LIVED, THERE.` · `HUMILITY, THEN RESPONSIBILITY.` · then, large: `EVERYONE ON ONE SPECK.`

segments.voice: Picture the photo: a dark field, a slanting band of light, and in it one pale dot. Remember, one at a time, that someone you love is on it, someone you're angry with is on it, you are on it, and so is everyone who ever lived. Rest your attention on the dot, and breathe.
Sagan. The astronomer who wrote about Earth as a pale blue dot, a speck in a sunbeam holding everyone. Today's word.
Your line: everyone on one speck. The driver who cut you off, the stranger online: they're on it too. That's day one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Some people, religious and not, keep the Pale Blue Dot photograph as a reminder of scale, and teachers, scientists and faith leaders have used it to talk about humility and care for the earth.

what a scholar hears: part of the Family Portrait, a mosaic of about sixty frames, the last images Voyager 1 took before its cameras went dark.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the Sagan paraphrase tracked his copyrighted passage too closely (everyone you love, every king and peasant, a mote of dust in a sunbeam, no help from elsewhere, our only home); rewritten in clearly different words, and the carry's 'only home' removed. 'No scientific purpose at all' softened to 'little'; 'one of the most famous photographs ever taken' cut; howItsDone softened.

Sagan's 1994 passage is under copyright and is paraphrased only, in deliberately different wording; the 'responsibility' paraphrase (no sign help will come from elsewhere; be kinder to one another) follows his argument closely, so a Keeper should check it reads as paraphrase, not quotation.

Facts to confirm: February 14, 1990; about 6 billion km (3.7 billion miles); Earth about 0.12 pixel; Family Portrait of about 60 frames; these were Voyager 1's last images; Voyager 1 launched in 1977.
'No scientific purpose' is a common description; some at NASA saw minor value. Confirm framing.
